title: The Covenants That Hold the Bible Together
subtitle: A guide to the biblical covenants and covenant theology, tracing the promises God made to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David, and how they all find their fulfillment in the new covenant in Christ

sections.title: One Story, Not Sixty Six Books
sections.body:
Most Christians read the Bible as a drawer full of loose pieces. A law here, a story there, a psalm, a letter, a strange vision at the end. They believe it is one book the way you believe a thing you have been told but never seen. The unity stays abstract.

The covenants are how the Bible holds together. They are the spine running down the back of the whole story.

A covenant is a binding relationship that God establishes by promise. He commits himself, names the terms, and seals it with a sign. From Noah to Abraham to Moses to David and on to the new covenant in Christ, these are not separate religions stacked end to end. They are chapters in one unfolding commitment, each building on the last, all of them straining toward the same end. Learn to trace them and the Bible stops being a drawer of pieces. It becomes a single, deliberate, advancing story with God as its author. Miss them and you will always read in fragments.

sections.title: Noah and the World Held Open
sections.body:
After the flood, God makes the first named covenant in Scripture. He sets his bow in the clouds and swears never again to destroy the earth by water. It is a covenant with Noah, and through him with every living creature, and even with the ground itself.

This is grace before there is law. God binds himself to a world that has just proven it deserves judgment.

The Noahic covenant buys time. It holds the world open, stable, seasons turning, so that the larger plan of redemption has a stage to play out on. Every sunrise you have ever seen is a kept promise to a drowned world. And it tells you something about the God of the rest of the Bible. He is a covenant maker before he is a law giver. He commits first. He guarantees the ground beneath the whole story before he asks anything of anyone standing on it. Read Noah and you learn the shape of every covenant to come.

sections.title: Abraham and the Promise That Carries Everything
sections.body:
Then God calls one man out of a pagan city and makes him a staggering set of promises. A people. A land. A blessing that would reach every family on earth. The covenant with Abraham is the engine of the rest of the Bible, and Paul says the gospel itself was preached to Abraham in advance.

Notice how it is sealed. God puts Abraham to sleep and passes between the pieces alone. The covenant rests on God's faithfulness, not the patriarch's.

That is the heart of it. Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness, which is the verse Paul builds the whole doctrine of justification on. The promise to bless every family on earth is not fulfilled in Israel alone. It is fulfilled in Israel's greatest son, in whom the nations are blessed at last. When you read of Abraham you are reading the seed of the gospel. Every later covenant is an outworking of what God swore to one old man under the stars.

sections.title: Moses, the Law, and the Throne of David
sections.body:
At Sinai, God gives the covenant of law to the nation he rescued from Egypt. The law was never a way to earn the promise. It was the household order for a people already redeemed, showing them how to live as the people of a holy God, and exposing how far short they fell.

Then, generations later, God makes a covenant with David. A son of David would sit on a throne that never ends.

The Mosaic covenant reveals the holiness no Israelite could match, and so it teaches the nation to long for help from outside itself. The Davidic covenant fixes that longing on a coming King. Put them together and the Old Testament becomes a people who know the law they cannot keep and await the King who will. Both covenants ache toward someone who has not yet come. The law cannot save them. The throne stands empty of its final occupant. The whole story leans forward, waiting.

sections.title: The New Covenant Where They All Arrive
sections.body:
Jeremiah, in the rubble of a failed nation, hears God promise something new. A covenant not written on stone but on the heart. Sins remembered no more. God known by all his people, from the least to the greatest.

At a table on the night he was betrayed, Jesus lifted a cup and said this is the new covenant in my blood. The waiting was over.

Everything converges there. The world held open for Noah was held open for this. The blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations through this. The law of Moses is kept and the curse of it carried by this man. The throne of David is filled by this King forever. The new covenant does not cancel the others. It gathers them up and keeps them, sealed not with the blood of bulls but with the blood of the Son. Read the cup at that table and you are watching every covenant in the Bible come home.

sections.title: Read With the Spine in View
sections.body:
So here is how the covenants change your reading. You stop asking only what a passage means in itself and start asking where it sits in the story. Which covenant is this. What has God already promised. What is he still reaching toward.

Not a drawer of pieces. A single line of promise, advancing, kept.

I have preached individual texts for years before I learned to read them along this spine, and I preached them smaller than they were. A verse cut out of the covenant story is a verse you can twist into almost anything. A verse read in its place in the story preaches itself. The God who set a bow in the clouds, who passed between the pieces, who gave the law and raised the throne, kept every word of it at a cross and an empty tomb. Learn the covenants, and you will never read the Bible as fragments again.
